docs.text:
This is the week where C++ shows its systems-language roots. We'll look at how objects sit in memory, how pointers work, what goes wrong with manual memory management (and why modern C++ rarely does it), how text is stored, and how to manipulate individual bits.

It's also the week where we meet undefined behaviour properly. Don't worry — the goal isn't to scare you, it's to give you a clear map of where the cliffs are, so you can walk confidently everywhere else.

# Lesson Standard Length 3.1 Arrays: C arrays, std::array, and a first look at std::span C++20 10 min 3.2 Pointers: addresses, arithmetic, and const C++20 12 min 3.3 Dynamic memory and a first map of undefined behaviour C++20 12 min 3.4 Strings: C strings, std::string, and std::string_view C++23 12 min 3.5 Bits and bytes: bitwise operators, std::byte, and C++23 11 min

When you're done with the lessons, take the week quiz and the programming assignment.

docs.title: Week 3 programming assignment: A bit-packed sensor record
docs.text:
A sensor sends 32-bit records: bits 0–11 are a temperature reading (unsigned, 0.1°C steps with an offset of -40°C), bits 12–19 humidity (percent), bits 20–27 a sensor id, bits 28–31 flags.

  1. Write constexpr std::uint32_t pack(...) and Record unpack(std::uint32_t).
  2. Take a std::span<const std::uint32_t> of records and print each one.
  3. Report how many records have flag bit 0 set, using std::popcount or masks.
  4. No raw new, no C strings, no reinterpret_cast.
Reference solution examples/week03/assignment_solution.cpp
#include <array>
#include <bit>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>

struct Record { double temp_c; unsigned humidity, id, flags; };

constexpr std::uint32_t pack(double temp_c, unsigned humidity, unsigned id, unsigned flags) {
    const auto raw_t = static_cast<std::uint32_t>((temp_c + 40.0) * 10.0 + 0.5) & 0xFFFu;
    return raw_t | (std::uint32_t{humidity & 0xFFu} << 12) | (std::uint32_t{id & 0xFFu} << 20)
           | (std::uint32_t{flags & 0xFu} << 28);
}

Record unpack(std::uint32_t r) {
    return {static_cast<double>(r & 0xFFFu) / 10.0 - 40.0, (r >> 12) & 0xFFu, (r >> 20) & 0xFFu, (r >> 28) & 0xFu};
}

int count_flag0(std::span<const std::uint32_t> recs) {
    int n = 0;
    for (auto r : recs) n += static_cast<int>((r >> 28) & 1u);
    return n;
}

int main() {
    constexpr std::array<std::uint32_t, 3> recs{pack(21.5, 40, 7, 0b0001), pack(-5.0, 85, 8, 0b0010),
                                                pack(36.6, 55, 9, 0b1001)};
    static_assert(pack(0.0, 0, 0, 0) == 400);   // checked at compile time
    for (auto r : recs) {
        const auto x = unpack(r);
        std::cout << "id=" << x.id << " temp=" << x.temp_c << "C hum=" << x.humidity
                  << "% flags=" << x.flags << " (" << std::popcount(x.flags) << " set)\n";
    }
    std::cout << "flag0 set in " << count_flag0(recs) << " records\n";
}

Output:

id=7 temp=21.5C hum=40% flags=1 (1 set)
id=8 temp=-5C hum=85% flags=2 (1 set)
id=9 temp=36.6C hum=55% flags=9 (2 set)
flag0 set in 2 records

docs.title: Lesson 3.1: Arrays: C arrays, std::array, and a first look at std::span
docs.text: C++20 · about 10 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Audio and video code is full of fixed-size buffers: a 1024-sample FFT window, a 16-entry lookup table, a 4×4 matrix. Arrays are the simplest container there is — but C-style arrays have a nasty habit of forgetting their own size the moment you pass them to a function. Let's see the problem and the modern fixes.

docs.title: C arrays, and how they forget their size
docs.text:
int window[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};
std::cout << sizeof(window);     // 16: the whole array (4 * sizeof(int))

void f(int a[4]) {               // looks like an array parameter...
    std::cout << sizeof(a);      // 8: it's really `int* a`!
}

When you pass a C array to a function, it decays to a pointer to its first element. The size is gone — the [4] in the parameter is ignored. This is where countless buffer overflows begin.

docs.title: std::array: an array that behaves like a value
docs.text: std::array<int, 4> is a thin wrapper around a C array with zero overhead. It knows its size, can be copied and compared, and can be returned from functions.

docs.title: std::span: "a view of some contiguous elements" (C++20)
docs.text:
When a function just needs to look at a sequence of elements, take a std::span<const T>. A span is a pointer plus a length; it doesn't own anything. It accepts C arrays, std::array, and std::vector alike — and it can't forget its size.

examples/week03/lesson01.cpp
#include <array>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <span>
#include <vector>

// One function works for C arrays, std::array and std::vector.
double mean(std::span<const float> xs) {
    if (xs.empty()) return 0.0;
    return std::accumulate(xs.begin(), xs.end(), 0.0) / static_cast<double>(xs.size());
}

void apply_gain(std::span<float> xs, float g) {
    for (auto& x : xs) x *= g;
}

int main() {
    float c_array[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};
    std::array<float, 4> arr{1, 2, 3, 4};
    std::vector<float> vec{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6};

    std::cout << "sizeof(c_array)=" << sizeof(c_array) << " std::size(c_array)=" << std::size(c_array) << '\n';
    std::cout << mean(c_array) << ' ' << mean(arr) << ' ' << mean(vec) << '\n';

    apply_gain(std::span(vec).subspan(2, 2), 10.0f);   // only elements 2 and 3
    for (float x : vec) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';

    std::array<float, 4> copy = arr;   // std::array copies like a value
    std::cout << std::boolalpha << (copy == arr) << '\n';
    try {
        std::cout << arr.at(10) << '\n';
    } catch (const std::out_of_range&) {
        std::cout << "at(10) threw out_of_range\n";
    }
}

Output:

sizeof(c_array)=16 std::size(c_array)=4
2.5 2.5 3.5
1 2 30 40 5 6 
true
at(10) threw out_of_range

docs.title: Bounds
docs.text:
a[i] with i out of range is undefined behaviour — no exception, no guaranteed crash. std::array and std::vector offer .at(i) which throws std::out_of_range. In debug builds you can also turn on library assertions (-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS for libstdc++, hardening modes in libc++) to catch bad operator[] indexes; many distributions enable that by default now.

Pro tip

Rule of thumb: own data with std::array / std::vector; pass it to functions as std::span<const T> (read) or std::span<T> (write). We'll revisit spans and mdspan in Week 10.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • C arrays decay to pointers when passed to functions and lose their size.
  • std::array<T, N> is a zero-overhead fixed array with value semantics.
  • Pass contiguous data as std::span<const T> / std::span<T> — one signature for all containers.
  • Out-of-bounds [] is UB; .at() throws; library hardening catches it in debug builds.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. Inside void f(int a[10]), what is sizeof(a) on a 64-bit system?

Show answer

8 — the parameter is actually int*; the 10 is ignored.

Q2. Does std::span own its elements?

Show answer

No. It is a non-owning view (pointer + size). The underlying storage must outlive the span.

Q3. What's the difference between arr[10] and arr.at(10) for a std::array<int, 4>?

Show answer

arr[10] is undefined behaviour; arr.at(10) throws std::out_of_range.

docs.title: Lesson 3.2: Pointers: addresses, arithmetic, and const
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Pointers have a scary reputation, but the idea is simple: a pointer is a variable that holds the address of another object. Android's NDK APIs, every C library, and hardware registers all speak in pointers, so you need to be fluent. Let's build the picture step by step.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
int level = 42;
int* p = &level;   // p holds the address of level
*p = 7;            // dereference: "the object p points to" -> level is now 7

Draw it as a box (level, containing 42) and an arrow (p) pointing at it. Unlike a reference, a pointer can be null (point at nothing) and can be re-pointed to another object.

Reference T& Pointer T* can be null no yes (nullptr) can be re-seated no yes syntax to use like the object *p, p->member use when always refers to something "optional" object, or re-pointing, or C APIs

docs.title: Pointer arithmetic
docs.text: If p points into an array, p + 1 points to the next element (not the next byte). p[i] is exactly *(p + i). Arithmetic is only valid within the same array (and one-past-the-end); going outside is UB.

docs.title: const and pointers: read right to left
docs.text:
const int* a;        // pointer to const int: can't modify *a, can re-point a
int* const b = &x;   // const pointer to int: can modify *b, can't re-point b
const int* const c = &x;  // neither

Trick: read the declaration right-to-left. int* const b = "b is a const pointer to int".

examples/week03/lesson02.cpp
#include <iostream>

struct Frame { int width; int height; };

void describe(const Frame* f) {       // pointer: may be null
    if (f == nullptr) { std::cout << "no frame\n"; return; }
    std::cout << f->width << 'x' << f->height << '\n';   // f->width == (*f).width
}

int main() {
    int level = 42;
    int* p = &level;
    *p = 7;
    std::cout << "level=" << level << '\n';

    int samples[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
    int* first = samples;              // array decays to pointer to first element
    int* last = samples + 4;
    std::cout << "*(first+2)=" << *(first + 2) << " first[3]=" << first[3]
              << " distance=" << (last - first) << '\n';

    for (const int* it = samples; it != samples + 5; ++it)   // one-past-the-end is OK to form
        std::cout << *it << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';

    const int* ro = &level;   // can't write through ro
    ro = &samples[0];         // but can re-point it
    int* const fixed = &level;
    *fixed = 99;              // can write, can't re-point
    std::cout << *ro << ' ' << level << '\n';

    Frame hd{1280, 720};
    describe(&hd);
    describe(nullptr);
}

Output:

level=7
*(first+2)=30 first[3]=40 distance=4
10 20 30 40 50 
10 99
1280x720
no frame

docs.title: The wrong way: dereferencing null or dangling pointers
docs.text:
int* p = nullptr;
*p = 1;              // UB: often a crash (SIGSEGV), but not guaranteed

int* q;
{ int local = 5; q = &local; }
*q = 6;              // UB: local is dead, q dangles

The fix is mostly design: prefer references when null isn't meaningful, keep pointers non-owning (owning pointers are smart pointers — Week 12), and don't let a pointer outlive what it points to.

About void*

void* can hold any object address but has no type. C APIs (like pthread_create or JNI) use it for "user data". In C++ code, prefer templates or std::function, and when you must use void*, static_cast it back to the exact original type.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • A pointer stores an address; *p is the object, &x is the address of x.
  • Pointer arithmetic moves by whole elements and is only valid within one array (plus one-past-the-end).
  • Read pointer declarations right to left: const int* vs int* const.
  • Use references when there's always an object; raw pointers for optional, non-owning access.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. If int a[4] starts at address 1000 and sizeof(int)==4, what address is a + 3?

Show answer

1012 — arithmetic is in units of elements.

Q2. Which of these can you do with const char* s: s = other; / *s = 'x';?

Show answer

s = other; is fine (re-pointing). *s = 'x'; is an error (the pointee is const).

Q3. When would you choose a pointer parameter over a reference?

Show answer

When "no object" is a legitimate input (null), or for C interop. Otherwise a reference documents that an object is required.

Q4. Is forming the pointer a + 4 for int a[4] UB? Dereferencing it?

Show answer

Forming one-past-the-end is allowed (used as an end marker); dereferencing it is UB.

docs.title: Lesson 3.3: Dynamic memory and a first map of undefined behaviour
docs.text: C++20 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Sometimes you don't know until run time how much memory you need — a frame whose size comes from a video header, say. That memory comes from the heap. C++ lets you manage it by hand with new and delete... and this lesson is mostly about why you almost never should. Seeing the failure modes once will make you appreciate RAII and smart pointers in the coming weeks.

docs.title: Stack vs heap
docs.text:
• Stack (automatic storage): local variables. Allocation is just moving a pointer — extremely fast — and cleanup is automatic at the end of scope. But it's limited (often 1–8 MB per thread) and sizes are fixed at compile time.
  • Heap (dynamic storage): new asks the allocator for memory at run time. You decide when it's freed.
int* one = new int{5};        // allocate one int
delete one;                   // free it

int* many = new int[n]{};     // allocate n ints, zeroed
delete[] many;                // arrays need delete[]

docs.title: Four ways manual memory goes wrong
docs.text:
1. Leak: forget to delete (or an early return/exception skips it).
  2. Double free: delete the same pointer twice.
  3. Use-after-free: use memory after deleting it.
  4. Mismatch: new[] with delete (or malloc with delete).

The last three are undefined behaviour.

docs.title: What "undefined behaviour" really means
docs.text:
UB doesn't mean "crashes" or "gives a random value". It means the standard places no requirements on the program at all. The optimizer assumes UB never happens and transforms code accordingly. So a single out-of-bounds read can make an unrelated if vanish. Common sources you've met so far:

  • signed integer overflow, out-of-bounds access, null/dangling dereference,
  • reading uninitialized variables, data races (Week 13), violating aliasing rules (Week 16).

We keep a full catalogue in Lesson 9.5.

docs.title: The fix: let objects own memory
docs.text:
Here's the modern answer. You rarely write new at all:

examples/week03/lesson03.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Frame {
    int w, h;
    std::vector<unsigned char> pixels;
    Frame(int w_, int h_) : w(w_), h(h_), pixels(static_cast<std::size_t>(w_ * h_)) {}
};

int main() {
    // Manual (the old way): works, but every exit path must remember delete[].
    int n = 4;
    int* raw = new int[n]{};
    raw[0] = 1;
    delete[] raw;

    // Modern: containers and smart pointers own memory.
    std::vector<int> v(static_cast<std::size_t>(n));   // n zeroed ints, freed automatically
    v[0] = 1;
    auto frame = std::make_unique<Frame>(640, 480);    // heap object, freed automatically
    std::cout << "frame " << frame->w << 'x' << frame->h << " bytes=" << frame->pixels.size()
              << " v[0]=" << v[0] << '\n';
}   // frame and v cleaned up here, in reverse order

Output:

frame 640x480 bytes=307200 v[0]=1

std::vector and std::unique_ptr free their memory automatically when they go out of scope — even if an exception is thrown. That's RAII, the heart of Week 4.

docs.title: Tools that catch memory bugs
docs.text:
Compile with AddressSanitizer while developing:

g++ -std=c++20 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined bug.cpp && ./a.out

ASan reports use-after-free, double free, out-of-bounds and leaks with a stack trace. Here's a program with a deliberate use-after-free. Our checker runs it under ASan in CI to make sure ASan really catches it:

Deliberately buggy

CI runs this under -fsanitize=address and checks the sanitizer reports the bug.

examples/week03/lesson03_uaf.cpp
// Deliberately broken: use-after-free. Compile with -fsanitize=address to see the report.
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int* p = new int{42};
    delete p;
    std::cout << *p << '\n';   // UB: heap-use-after-free
}

ASan prints something like ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free ... READ of size 4. Android supports ASan and HWASan too (HWASan is the recommended one on arm64).

Honest note

Valgrind and sanitizers find bugs in the code paths you execute. They're not proofs. Combine them with tests (Week 15) and with designs where ownership is obvious.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Stack allocation is fast and automatic; heap allocation is flexible but must be freed.
  • Manual new/delete invites leaks, double frees, use-after-free and mismatched delete[].
  • UB means no requirements at all; the optimizer assumes it never happens.
  • Let std::vector / std::unique_ptr own memory, and develop with -fsanitize=address,undefined.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What's wrong with int* p = new int[10]; delete p;?

Show answer

Memory from new[] must be released with delete[]; using delete is undefined behaviour.

Q2. Why can't you rely on UB 'just crashing'?

Show answer

The standard imposes no requirements; the optimizer may assume UB is impossible and transform surrounding code, so the effect can be anything, including silently wrong results.

Q3. Which tool reports heap-use-after-free with a stack trace?

Show answer

AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address), or HWASan on arm64 Android; also Valgrind's memcheck.

docs.title: Lesson 3.4: Strings: C strings, std::string, and std::string_view
docs.text: C++23 · about 12 minutes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Text is everywhere: file paths, log messages, codec names, JSON. C++ inherited C's strings — arrays of char ending in a zero byte — and they've caused more security bugs than almost anything else. Modern C++ gives you std::string to own text and std::string_view to look at it cheaply. Let's see when to use which.

docs.title: C strings: an array and a promise
docs.text:
"hello" is an array of 6 const chars: h e l l o \0. Every C string function (strlen, strcpy, strcat) walks until it finds that \0. If it's missing, or the destination buffer is too small, you overflow memory. strlen is also O(n) every time you call it.

char buf[8];
std::strcpy(buf, "much too long");   // WRONG: buffer overflow, UB

docs.title: std::string: owns its characters
docs.text: std::string stores its length, grows as needed, and frees its memory automatically. Short strings (typically up to 15 characters in libstdc++, 22 in libc++) are stored inside the string object with no heap allocation: the small string optimization (SSO).

docs.title: std::string_view: a window onto characters (C++17)
docs.text:
A string_view is just a pointer + length. It doesn't own anything, never allocates, and can view a std::string, a C string literal, or part of either. It's the ideal type for read-only string parameters:

bool is_audio(std::string_view mime) { return mime.starts_with("audio/"); }
is_audio("audio/opus");          // no std::string created
is_audio(some_std_string);       // no copy
examples/week03/lesson04.cpp
#include <cstring>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

using namespace std::literals;   // for "..."s and "..."sv

bool is_audio(std::string_view mime) { return mime.starts_with("audio/"); }

std::string_view extension(std::string_view path) {   // returns a view INTO path: caller keeps path alive
    const auto dot = path.rfind('.');
    return dot == std::string_view::npos ? std::string_view{} : path.substr(dot + 1);
}

int main() {
    const char* c = "hello";
    std::cout << "strlen=" << std::strlen(c) << " sizeof(\"hello\")=" << sizeof("hello") << '\n';

    std::string s = "track";
    s += "-01";                       // grows as needed
    s.insert(0, "my-");
    std::cout << s << " size=" << s.size() << '\n';

    std::cout << std::boolalpha << is_audio("audio/opus") << ' ' << is_audio(std::string{"video/h264"}) << '\n';

    const std::string path = "/sdcard/Music/song.flac";
    std::cout << "ext=" << extension(path) << '\n';

    auto owned = "literal"s;        // std::string
    auto view = "literal"sv;        // std::string_view
    std::cout << owned.size() << ' ' << view.size() << ' ' << (owned == view) << '\n';
    std::cout << "contains 'song'? " << path.contains("song") << '\n';   // C++23
}

Output:

strlen=5 sizeof("hello")=6
my-track-01 size=11
true false
ext=flac
7 7 true
contains 'song'? true

docs.title: The big pitfall: string_view doesn't keep anything alive
docs.text:
std::string_view codec_name() {
    std::string s = "opus";
    return s;                    // WRONG: view into a destroyed string
}
std::string_view v = std::string("tmp") + "x";   // WRONG: the temporary dies at the ';'

Rule: use string_view for parameters and short-lived local views; return and store std::string unless you're returning a view into something that clearly outlives the caller (like a string literal or a member).

Also: a string_view isn't NUL-terminated

sv.data() isn't guaranteed to end in \0, so don't pass it to C functions expecting a C string. Convert with std::string(sv).c_str() when calling C APIs.

We'll cover text formatting (std::format, std::print) and the hard truth about Unicode in Week 12.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • C strings rely on a terminating \0; strcpy-style functions easily overflow.
  • std::string owns and manages text; short strings avoid heap allocation (SSO).
  • Take read-only text parameters as std::string_view.
  • Never return or store a string_view to something that may die first.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. What is sizeof("abc")?

Show answer

4: three characters plus the terminating \0.

Q2. Why is std::string_view a good parameter type but a risky member/return type?

Show answer

As a parameter it avoids copies and accepts any string type, and the argument outlives the call. As a return/member it may outlive the characters it views, producing a dangling view.

Q3. Can you pass sv.data() to fopen?

Show answer

Not safely: a string_view's data isn't guaranteed to be NUL-terminated. Make a std::string first.

docs.title:
Lesson 3.5: Bits and bytes: bitwise operators, std::byte, and

C++23 · about 11 minutes
Why this matters
docs.text: An H.264 NAL unit header packs three fields into a single byte: 1 bit, 2 bits and 5 bits. Hardware registers, flags, compression, hashing — all of it is bit twiddling. C++ gives you direct access to bits, and C++20 finally added a proper <bit> header so you no longer need compiler-specific builtins. Let's decode that header.

docs.title: The operators
docs.text:
Op Meaning Typical use a & b AND test/clear bits with a mask a \| b OR set bits a ^ b XOR toggle bits ~a NOT invert (build "clear" masks) a << n, a >> n shift move fields into place

Extracting a field = shift it down, then mask it: (byte >> 5) & 0b11 gives bits 5–6.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Shifting by a count >= the width of the (promoted) type is UB: 1u << 32 on a 32-bit unsigned.
  • 1 << 31 on int: before C++20 this was UB; since C++20 signed integers are defined to be two's complement and left shift is well-defined — but stick to unsigned types for bit manipulation anyway.
  • Remember integer promotion: ~std::uint8_t{0x0F} is an int 0xFFFFFFF0, not 0xF0.

docs.title: std::byte (C++17)
docs.text: std::byte is "a byte of raw memory", not a character and not a number. It only supports bitwise ops, so you can't accidentally do arithmetic on it. Use std::to_integer<int>(b) to read it.

docs.title: <bit> (C++20)
docs.text:
Portable versions of things you used to need intrinsics for: std::popcount, std::countl_zero, std::countr_zero, std::rotl/rotr, std::has_single_bit (power of two?), std::bit_ceil, std::bit_width, and std::bit_cast — the safe way to reinterpret an object's bits as another type of the same size. C++23 added std::byteswap, and std::endian (C++20) tells you the platform byte order.

examples/week03/lesson05.cpp
#include <bit>
#include <bitset>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

struct NalHeader { unsigned forbidden, ref_idc, type; };

NalHeader parse(std::uint8_t b) {
    return {static_cast<unsigned>(b >> 7) & 0x1u,
            static_cast<unsigned>(b >> 5) & 0x3u,
            static_cast<unsigned>(b) & 0x1Fu};
}

int main() {
    const std::uint8_t nal = 0x67;   // a typical H.264 SPS header byte
    const auto h = parse(nal);
    std::cout << "bits=" << std::bitset<8>(nal) << " forbidden=" << h.forbidden
              << " ref_idc=" << h.ref_idc << " type=" << h.type << '\n';

    unsigned flags = 0;
    flags |= 1u << 3;        // set bit 3
    flags |= 1u << 0;        // set bit 0
    flags &= ~(1u << 0);     // clear bit 0
    flags ^= 1u << 5;        // toggle bit 5
    std::cout << "flags=" << std::bitset<8>(flags) << " popcount=" << std::popcount(flags) << '\n';

    std::cout << "bit_ceil(600)=" << std::bit_ceil(600u) << " has_single_bit(512)=" << std::has_single_bit(512u)
              << " countr_zero(40)=" << std::countr_zero(40u) << '\n';

    std::cout << std::hex << "bits of 1.0f = 0x" << std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(1.0f)
              << " byteswap(0x11223344)=0x" << std::byteswap(0x11223344u) << std::dec << '\n';
    std::cout << "little endian? " << (std::endian::native == std::endian::little) << '\n';

    std::byte b{0b1010'0000};
    b |= std::byte{0x01};
    std::cout << "std::byte as int: " << std::to_integer<int>(b) << '\n';
}

Output:

bits=01100111 forbidden=0 ref_idc=3 type=7
flags=00101000 popcount=2
bit_ceil(600)=1024 has_single_bit(512)=1 countr_zero(40)=3
bits of 1.0f = 0x3f800000 byteswap(0x11223344)=0x44332211
little endian? 1
std::byte as int: 161

docs.title: The wrong way to reinterpret bits
docs.text:
float f = 1.0f;
std::uint32_t u = *reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t*>(&f);   // WRONG: violates strict aliasing (UB)
std::uint32_t ok = std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(f);          // right (C++20); or std::memcpy

Pro tip: ring buffers love powers of two

If a buffer's capacity is a power of two, index & (capacity - 1) replaces the slower index % capacity. You'll use exactly this in the embedded capstone.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
Key takeaways

  • Extract a bit field with shift-then-mask; use unsigned types for bit manipulation.
  • Shifting by >= the type width is UB; watch integer promotion with ~ on small types.
  • std::byte is raw memory, not a number; <bit> gives portable popcount, rotations, bit_cast etc.
  • Use std::bit_cast or memcpy, never reinterpret_cast, to reinterpret an object's bits.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Q1. How do you extract bits 2..4 (3 bits) of x?

Show answer

(x >> 2) & 0b111.

Q2. What is the type and value of ~std::uint8_t{0}?

Show answer

int, value -1 (all bits set), due to integer promotion before ~.

Q3. Why is *reinterpret_cast<int*>(&some_float) wrong?

Show answer

It violates the strict aliasing rule (accessing a float object through an int glvalue), which is UB. Use std::bit_cast<int>(f) or std::memcpy.

Q4. What does std::has_single_bit(x) tell you?

Show answer

Whether x is a power of two.

(x >> 2) & 0b111.

Q10. (from 3.5) What is the type and value of ~std::uint8_t{0}?

Show answer

int, value -1 (all bits set), due to integer promotion before ~.
